# 2. Children of Grungni

*Pages PDF 26-37*

## **Children of Grungni**
Roleplaying a DwaRf 

Dwarfs are an exceptionally proud, ancient species known for their craftsmanship, steadfastness, dour disposition, battle prowess and ale-guzzling. Broadly speaking, there are three types of Dwarfs who civilly interact with humans. The first and most numerous are the Karak Dwarfs who dwell in the mountains. The second type of Dwarf are the ones who live among manlings. As the vast majority of these reside within the borders of the Empire, they are known as Imperial Dwarfs. The third and least encountered are the Norse Dwarfs, who are more likely encountered in the seaports located on or riverports near the Sea of Claws. 

## **Cultural Values**
The Dwarf way of life has changed little in the culture’s seven and a half millennia of existence. Karak, Imperial, and Norse Dwarfs continue to share the same basic cultural values. Dwarfs respect age, wealth, skill, reputation, and honour above all else. Those who possess all five virtues command the greatest respect among their people and are their leaders. 

Respect for tradition is also important, though circumstances for Dwarfs living among manlings have resulted in some degree of divergence from traditions held sacred by Karak and Norse Dwarfs. Still, the lack of respect for tradition is seen as a fault rather than its presence being considered a virtue. 

## **Age**
In Dwarf culture, age is considered the most reliable indicator of a Dwarf ’s wisdom. Long years of toil and loss often temper the brashness and misplaced confidence of youth. Decades of labour leave older Dwarfs with a wealth of experience-based knowledge and understanding to render sound judgement and insight to the younger members of their clans. 

While some young Dwarfs require the hard lessons of life to temper their fiery spirit, most have the sense to take heed of their elders and learn from them. 

Older Dwarfs do not teach younger clan members by lecturing them. Instead, they impart their wisdom through tales of deeds and consequence, whether such was personally experienced by the Dwarf relating the story or something they were taught in their own youth. By this method, deeds of past and recent ancestors are kept alive as life lessons. 

The length and fullness of a Dwarf ’s beard (or hair, in the case of Dwarf women) is the primary indicator of age and wisdom a Dwarf has. The greyness in a Dwarf ’s beard or hair is of lesser consideration as Dwarfs do not uniformly turn grey. 

## **Wealth**
Critics often claim — discreetly, out of earshot — that Dwarfs are a miserly and avaricious species. The truth of the matter is that Dwarf culture values prosperity, and individual Dwarfs often measure success by the wealth they have managed to accumulate. In turn, Dwarfs consider wealth as a means to a comfortable life and respect of their fellows. 

Typically, Dwarfs are wealthier than their counterparts of other species.  For example, Jaan van der Kuypers of Marienburg is indisputably the richest manling in the Old World. Yet, even his fabulous wealth pales by comparison to that of even a minor Dwarf King. 

Though typically possessive of their wealth, Dwarfs can be very generous when bestowing valuable gifts to honoured members of the clan. Dwarfs also show great generosity in repaying debts and rewarding friendships and firm allies with proven virtues. 

When a Dwarf dies, they are buried with few highly prized possessions, mostly items that represent their accomplishments and standing within the clan. Dwarfs passing from the world leave much of their wealth to be divided among their kin and so pass it from one generation to another. In this way, a Dwarf ’s hoard of treasure is not only a mark of wealth and security, but also a link to their revered ancestors of past generations. 

By dedicating themselves to mastering their craft, Dwarfs honour not only their masters, but also their clan, ancestors, and the craft itself. Since all Dwarf crafts trace their origins to the Ancestor Gods, attaining mastery of one’s craft is as much a religious duty as it is a source of pride and honour. 

## **Craft Guilds**
## **Skill**
Dwarf attention to and memory for detail is unmatched by other species. They learn by keenly observing their masters at work, intently listening to the lore, and studiously applying their craft. Dwarfs mastering their craft eventually gain great respect from others in their respective clans and craft guilds. The greatest of Dwarf artisans attain a level of mastery that is unrivalled by any other species. 

**Craft Guild** is a term used when multiple clans of a Dwarf realm engage in the same craft. Unlike manling Guilds, craft guilds do not restrict the number of people working in a craft. Craft guilds also do not regulate prices or output. Examples of craft guilds include armourers and weaponsmiths, brewers, engineers, metalsmiths, and miners. 

## **Reputation**
Reputation is everything to a Dwarf. Wealth can come and go, many times outside the control of a Dwarf. In contrast, reputation is the only constant Dwarfs can count on in an ever-challenging world. Central to Dwarf reputation is the value of their word. 

Once given, a Dwarf ’s word is unbreakable and binds the individual to that oath. As a result, Dwarfs are very reluctant to give their word on anything. When pressed on the matter, Dwarfs choose their words carefully, almost like they were a slick Altdorf litigant. Examples of a typical turn of phrase would be, ‘I will do as you ask, unless something prevents me’ or ‘based on what you told me, I will do whatever is within my meagre abilities’. 

Such equivocation has led to Dwarfs gaining an undeserved reputation for evasiveness. Dwarfs know that their sense of honour requires that the obligation that comes from giving their word requires the oath to be fulfilled to the letter. Moreover, Dwarfs know that should they die with their oath unfulfilled, the responsibility then passes on to their descendants. Such consideration weighs heavily on Dwarfs considering giving their word. 

In extreme cases, Dwarfs who dishonourably fail to keep their oath forsake their clan and become Slayers. This drastic act serves to remove the stigma of a failed oath from the clan, as in death, a Slayer redeems their sullied honour. It also serves to prove that the clan takes their oaths seriously, as is only right proper. 

For outsiders, to be so presumptuous as to demand an oath from a Dwarf is considered to be a grave insult. Such an offence is not easily forgotten, much less forgiven. 

## **Honour**
The honour of Dwarfs is closely tied to their reputation. Honour is a code that directs how Dwarfs interact with one another, both within and without their clan. It also dictates how they interact with other species. 

Dwarfs are their most forthright and honest when dealing with members of their own clan. Trust among these closely-related members is very important to the cohesiveness and honour of the clan. 

Honour is also important when dealing with other clans within a Dwarf hold. Security of a Dwarf hold requires a high level of ethical behaviour between those living within and defending its walls. 

Honour among Imperial Dwarfs is not as stringent as it is among Karak and Norse Dwarfs. Centuries, even millennia, of living among manlings have modified the Dwarf sense of honour. Imperial Dwarfs who undertake roguish occupations or choose nominally dishonest work (such as Smuggler or Wrecker) do not feel the sense of shame that would drive Karak and Norse Dwarfs to becoming Slayers. Even so, Imperial Dwarf rogues very rarely prey upon their own people. 

## **Tradition**
Tradition is one of the bonds Dwarfs share with one another. It serves the purpose of uniting members of a clan as it does bring clans together within a Dwarf hold or settlement. 

Dwarfen traditions are as pragmatic as the Dwarfs themselves. Most of these tried and tested traditions were laid down by Dwarf ancestors and have existed for millennia. Dwarfs believe that any failure to honour tradition by properly behaving in the prescribed manner could lead to outcomes ranging from simple misfortune to utter disaster. 

Some traditions take on the form of a soft-spoken ritual invocation such as when Dwarf weaponsmiths call on the ancestors to inspire their hands in crafting superior axes or jewelsmiths to successfully work a delicate piece of jewellery. Other customs involve correctly reciting a traditional Dwarf story, which may include foundation tales for a specific Dwarf ritual. Certain days dedicated to remembering the deeds of one’s ancestors may involve story-telling or song during communal feasts. 

Traditions among Imperial Dwarfs tend to take on a more personal and private tone. This difference is largely due to the widespread distribution of many clans outside those that inhabit Imperial cities. Imperial Dwarf families become the focal point when clan gatherings are not practical. 

## **Beards and Hair**
The pride Dwarfs take in their beards is legendary. Beards are never cut or even trimmed. Instead, beards are continuously combed through to clear tangles and braided with care. Dwarfs only mar their beards in the most dire times. Chewing one’s beard is a sign of deepest grief, such as the loss of a loved one. Dwarfs who shave themselves acknowledge their complete loss of honour. Shaving is extremely rare even among Slayers. 

The act of forcibly shaving a Dwarf ’s beard is the most grievous and unforgivable insult imaginable. Millennia ago, the humiliation of a Dwarf ambassador forcibly shaved at the court of the Phoenix King in Ulthuan ignited the 500-year War of Vengeance between the High Elves and Dwarfs. 

Dwarf females do not have beards (despite rumours to the contrary), yet have thick hair which they comb, brush, and braid as much as males do their beards.  Dwarf female braids convey their status within the clan. The most elaborate braids are generally found among the noble clans of a Dwarf hold. 

## **Social Structure**
For a civilization to have endured as long as the Dwarfs, the social structure must be strong enough to continue unabated for many millennia, even in the face of adversities that have, at times, bordered on catastrophes. 

Dwarfs place a great deal of import on the wisdom of their elders and the example of their ancestors. It is in their nature to pay deference to older members of their clan, and the Khazalid term Gnollen-grom, the respect due to a Dwarf by virtue of his impressive beard, helps illustrate the cultural importance of reverence for experience. A Dwarf Beardling who fails to show proper regard for a Longbeard soon earns a reputation as a Wattock (failure), Wazzock (fool), or Wanaz (one who cannot cultivate a decent beard). Older Dwarfs lead younger Dwarfs in both peace and war, handing down their revered teachings to future generations. The most important of these lessons are the techniques and teachings endorsed or taught by the kings of ancient days, the clan’s ancestors, and the Ancestor Gods. In any society of Dwarfs it can be expected for young Dwarfs to look to their elders for advice, and for elder Dwarfs to look to the deeds of their forebears for inspiration and insight. 

## **Clan and Family**
Clan and family are central to a Dwarf ’s life. Like an extended family, the Throng (as clan members are collectively called) is bound to one another by blood and common ancestry. The families in a clan also share a common homeland, many dating back to the initial Dwarf settlements in the Worlds Edge and Dragonback Mountains while others count the time when their ancestors founded the Dwarf holds in the Vaults, Black, and Grey Mountains. Even Imperial Dwarf clans trace their ancestral homes to the mountain realms while Norse Dwarfs only consider the Dwarf holds in eastern Norsca. 

Dwarfs trace their ancestors through the millennia, even outstripping Halflings when it comes to genealogy. Committing the sagas of their ancestors to memory is as important to a Dwarf ’s education as mastering intricacies of their clan’s craft. Dwarfs take great pride in their ancestors’ achievements. Sagas are always written and recited in a straightforward, unboastful, and matterof-fact manner. From a Dwarf perspective, the deeds of venerated ancestors are glorious enough in themselves with little need to dress it up with finer words. 

Clan memory runs deep within Dwarfs and family obligations are taken seriously, even if generations old. An ancestor’s unresolved debts fall upon their descendants and remain for however long it takes for the descendants to pay in full. The continued support to the Empire is the example that illustrates this principle, arising as it does from Sigmar’s rescue of the Dwarf High King Kurgan Ironbeard from his Orc captors. There is also the example where any insult done to a Dwarf is considered an affront to the entire clan. In this situation, any clan member can be elected or take it upon themselves to take revenge  in order to redeem the clan’s honour. 

## **The Runesmith Clans**
One of the more important clans, the Runesmiths are descendants of Thungni, Ancestor God and the younger son of Grungni and Valaya. Only Runesmiths are capable of binding and incorporating the winds of magic into their works. Yet, not all members of the Runesmith clans have this gift. Few are very proficient at runesmithing and become full-fledged Runesmiths. 

Many other clan members have very limited ability to bind the winds of magic into runes, most of which are temporary or unique runes that have limited application.  Such clan members become the Priests (and Priestesses) of all the Ancestor Gods and dedicated their lives to ensuring Dwarfs learn and observe the traditions and rites laid down at the dawn of time. 

The majority of Runesmith clan Dwarfs have no ability to bind magic into runes. Instead, they fulfil the highly valued roles of keepers of Dwarf lore and law. Runescribes, Librarians, Archivists, and Loremasters all serve this important task within Dwarf society. These Dwarfs typically live in the Dwarf realms. 

Among Imperial Dwarfs, those from the Runesmith clans that do not have the ability to inscribe Runic Magic usually become skilled smiths in other professions (such as blacksmith, jewelsmith, or weaponsmith). All Imperial Dwarf Runesmith clan members are descended from the Thunder-stone clan of Karak Varn. 

## **Stages of Life**
Dwarfs age more slowly than manlings, although the difference is not as great in the former’s early years. Manlings become full grown between 16 and 18 years of age while Dwarfs do so between 18 and 20. On average, Dwarfs live three manling lifetimes and the undiminished vitality of an ageing Dwarf is seldom seen among humans. 

The Day of Naming, is traditionally the first day of a Dwarf ’s life. On this day, the newborn’s parents, clan elders, and all direct living ancestors present the infant at the temples of Grungni and Valaya to receive the blessings of the Ancestor Gods. At the Temple of Grungni, the birth and name of the infant is added to the Hold’s annals. Then taken to the Temple of Valaya the infant undergoes a ritual of welcome which includes passing them through the smoke of Valaya’s hearth and feeding them a spoonful of stone soup. Imperial Dwarfs only go to a Grungni temple for the complete ritual. 

Dwarfs are not considered adults until they reach 30 years. These ‘Young Beards’ or ‘Beardlings’ spend their childhood years learning their clan’s craft, traditions, place in Dwarf society, and combat training. Beardlings also spend a few years in the mines and the smithies learning about the earth and process to identify and purify metals. All Dwarfs are expected to partake in the defence of their Dwarf hold, town, village, or mining settlement. 

An important event for Dwarfs is entry into adulthood where the young Dwarf is formally present to the clan in the rite of _Kumenouht_ . Clans living in scattered communities usually wait until they gather on the Day of Remembrance to observe this rite of adulthood. Dwarfs reaching adulthood making an offering of a novice-piece which demonstrates the youngster’s skill in the clan’s craft and to honour the clan’s ancestors and Ancestor Gods. Examples are a young Dwarf from a brewer clan offering a barrel of dark beer while one from a jewelsmith clan would present a piece of jewellery or cut gemstones. The clan elders then present the Dwarf with their first set of tools and insignia of the clan’s craft guild.  Newly elevated, young adult Dwarfs begin to establish their reputation within the clan. They are elevated from novice to apprentice, but continue to hone their craft with more senior clan members. 

Young adult Karak and Norse Dwarfs who show limited aptitude within their craft have the option of joining their Dwarf hold’s garrison or standing army. 

Craft Guilds do not exist among Imperial Dwarf clans. In fact, due to the widespread distribution of some clans across several villages, Imperial Dwarf clans are not bound to a specific craft. Imperial Dwarfs from a brewing clan could opt to become a carpenter or soldier depending upon opportunity (and manling Guild rules). No Imperial Dwarf can elect to undertake careers involving Runic Magic unless they are a member of a Runesmith clan with the innate ability. 

Dwarfs reaching 70 years take on the status of Full Beards. They can take younger Dwarfs as apprentices. Should two or more Full Beards want to take on the same apprentice or if someone is not chosen by a Full Beard, then the clan elders intervene to resolve the situation. Full Beards may choose to further master their craft rather than take on any apprentices. 

Dwarfs reach the status of Longbeards when they reach 120. They are not yet regarded as Clan Elders, but Longbeards are respected for their wisdom, skill, and knowledge of clan traditions and crafts. In many cases, their reputations spread outside their craft guild, which enable Longbeards to receive commissions from outside clans. Many Longbeards continue to teach younger members of their craft guild. Others fully dedicate themselves to further mastering their craft. 

At 150, Dwarfs become Eldersof their clan and become part of its Elder Council by virtue of age, wisdom, and length of beard or hair. Elder Councils consider any matter that directly affects the clans and their interests, even judging violations of Dwarf law. If the issue at hand only involves members of a single clan family, then the Elder Council may do no more than recommend a course of action to the oldest member and head of the family. 

The few Dwarfs exceeding 200 years become a Great Beard and are held in high esteem by their clan. Their knowledge, experience, and insight make Great Beards very valuable during difficult and lean times. 

Rarely does a Dwarf live beyond 400 years, but those that manage such a feat become Living Ancestors and are venerated both as being blessed by the Ancestor Gods and symbols of their clan’s good fortunes. The vigour of Living Ancestors remains undiminished and contrasts sharply with the experience of very old manlings. Dwarfs resist referring to Living Ancestors as immortal, but it does seem that only injury or disease can threaten the life of a Living Ancestor. Dwarfs sometimes say that Living Ancestors are simply too stubborn to die. 

## **Death and Burial**
According to ancient lore, the earth gave birth to the Dwarfs and their deceased bodies must return to Valaya’s embrace. Meanwhile, the Dwarf spirit journeys to the world of their ancestors. Funeral rites performed by priests of Gazul, Ancestor God and protector of the Dwarf dead, facilitate this final journey. 

Dwarfs dying of old age sense their stamina and strength fading, thus knowing their end is near. A priest of Gazul is summoned so the dying Dwarf can name which of their possessions will accompany them to their tomb. The heirs are then summoned to witness the dying Dwarf ’s bequests, somewhat like the reading of a will among manlings, except the Dwarf is not yet dead. The Dwarf then spends the remainder of their days with family and friends. 

When death comes, the priest returns to take the deceased to the Temple of Gazul where it lies in repose for four days. The priest then inscribes runic protections on the body to ensure the spirit’s safe arrival to the Hall of Ancestors and prevent the corpse from being used for necromantic purposes. At the end of four days, the priest entombs the body in the clan’s burial vault with their personal items. He then reseals the vault with a rune to prevent any desecration until the next burial. 

Priests of Gazul accompany Dwarf armies to administer death-rites to the fallen. Slain Dwarfs are buried on site when returning the fallen to the Dwarf hold is impractical. In such cases, only the bodies of Kings, Runesmiths, and Clan Elders are returned for burial. 

## Importance of Grudges and Reckonings
Dwarfs place great importance on recalling every person who has shown them kindness and friendship. They also remember all those who have wronged them in some fashion, from slights to insult, war and betrayal. 

Any person who performs a great service to the Dwarf (such as saving his life) is henceforth considered a ‘Dwarf-friend’. As a result of their acts, Dwarf-friends gain a friendship with bonds so strong that it spans decades. The companionship of human poet Felix Jaeger and the trollslayer Gotrek Grunisson serve as a wellknown example. 

Wrongs and insults bring the full weight of Dwarf enmity on the perpetrator. Additionally, betrayal can change the status of a Dwarf-friend to a foe among Dwarfs. Dwarf grudges are nothing to take lightly. It might take a Dwarf years or decades to gain satisfaction, but they inevitably seek to gain their revenge. When the retribution comes, it takes whatever form the Dwarf finds appropriate, irrespective of what the target thinks. 

## **Book of Grudges**
Any insult, wrong, or betrayal against Dwarfs are ceremoniously entered into a Book of Grudges . Each Dwarf king keeps a Book of Grudges for any transgressions perpetrated against the Dwarf hold or the King’s clan. Dwarfs who have a proficiency for literacy usually keep their own personal Book of Grudges to augment their memory of wrongs done to them. An entered grudge can only be crossed out when Dwarf receives appropriate compensation or has extracted suitable vengeance. 

The Dwarf victory in the War of Vengeance satisfied many of recorded grudges against the Elves. High King Gotrek’s declaration that taking the life of, and Phoenix Crown from Caledor II of Ulthuan constituted just compensation for the rest of the Elf insults and injustices before and during the war. New grudges against Elves have since been added, but not as many as Dwarf interactions turned towards a different adversary. 

Dwarf contempt for Elves does not match their hatred of Greenskins. The bloodthirsty Orcs and scheming Goblins have slain more Dwarfs and destroyed more Dwarf holds than all other species combined. The High King’s Book of Grudges has a single entry regarding these most persistent of enemies. Only the full eradication of Orcs, Goblins, and their kin would satisfy the grudge. 

Dwarfs know that Skaven while manlings may speak of them as foul vermin of legend to scare wayward children. Skaven were involved in the fall of some of the Dwarf holds such as Karak Varn and Karak Eight Peaks. The Great Book of Grudges contains entries calling for the eradication of the loathsome Ratmen. The failure of the manlings to take this threat seriously is a source of bewildering consternation to most Dwarfs. 

A typical Book of Grudges has four columns: ‘Grudge’ (description of the wrong), ‘Grudge Against’ (naming the offender), ‘Date of Grudge’, and ‘Date Satisfied’.

## **Book of Remembrance**
## **Bugman’s Rangers**
Bugman’s Rangers are absolute terrors to Greenskin tribes living in vicinity of the Grey and Black Mountains, even travelling further afield in his quest for vengeance. Bugman’s grudge would be the epitome of Dwarf grudges. 

Long ago, Goblins destroyed Josef Bugman’s brewery near Wusterburg in (then) Sudenland during the Master Brewer’s absence. Upon seeing the ruins of the once full ale barrels, Bugman’s anger erupted and he swore an oath to end the Goblin tribes responsible. The oath was later amended to include all Orcs, Goblins, and related species. 

A battle-weary detachment of Bugman’s Rangers led by oneeyed Jorj Ruddle ambush Characters crossing one of the mountain ranges surrounding the Empire and capture them for interrogations. Once satisfied that the Characters are not spies for a local Greenskin tribe, Jorj recruits the Characters to reconnoitre a nearby village so the Rangers could stage a night attack. Should the Characters agree to help, Jorj promises to pay them handsomely. If the Characters agree to help as a ruse to escape the crazed Dwarfs, well, Bugman’s Rangers are very good and relentless trackers. 

In addition to the Book of Grudges, Clan Elders keep several other books for the clan. One such is the Book of Remembrance, a tome which lists the deeds and renown acts by the clan’s ancestors and, where applicable, those of living clan members. Entries in this book are read aloud to clan members when they gather on the Day of Remembrance in order to honour the great deeds of the clan. Sometimes these readings occur in conjunction with rites of adult passage for younger clan members. 

Like all other books in the clan’s possession, there are many Book of Remembrance volumes. All current books are locked away in hidden, secured locations near the Clan Elder. Past volumes are kept in the extensive Dwarf hold librarians. In Imperial Dwarf communities, books of the past are safely stored in secured underground vaults in the closest Temple of Grungni. 

## **Book of Debt**
Clan Elders are responsible for updating the clan’s Book of Debt ( _Baraz Kron_ ), which is essentially a ledger tracking the details and amounts of the clan’s debts. Maintaining the integrity of the book is a matter of pride. Debts can take multiple forms. 

The most common are simple financial debts, taken to fund some expensive endeavour or, by less fortunate Dwarfs, simply to make ends meet. Dwarfs are generally loathe to take on such debts, and move mountains to avoid doing so. Imperial Dwarfs forced to deal with manling moneylenders especially despise the practice, but all take pains to carefully record each repayment. 

Another type of debt is Honour Debts. Honour Debts are incurred when someone outside the clan provides a great service or favour to the clan. Dwarfs prefer to be the ones that are owed a favour or service and do not relish being in someone else’s debt. It’s one thing to be in debt to a Dwarf-friend, quite another to owe someone who does not have that honorific title. Dwarfs work hard to discharge Honour Debts as soon as practical. 

Clan Elders understand that the path to Slayer is opened should they fail to keep accurate records of the clan’s debts. This is more than enough incentive to ensure that the books are kept up-to-date. 

## **Book of Ancestors**
The Book of Ancestors ( _Gromthi Kron_ ) details the genealogy of the clan and closely-related clans to the present. The books are usually a series of large tomes, most of which stretch back millennia. Elders from closely-related clans frequently meet to ensure entries are consistent from one Book of Ancestors to the next. 

Dwarfs are meticulous record-keepers, which makes disputes extremely rare. Should a difference be unresolvable between parties, the involved clans bring in a local priest (preferably one of Valaya, but one of Grungni would do) to find a resolution. Elders only keep volumes of the Book of Ancestors from the past century readily available for update. Older books are secured at the local Temple of Valaya. 

Cult of Verena historians have made several unsuccessful attempts to obtain copies or review originals for genealogical reasons, or so they say. 

## Staples of the Dwarf Diet
A Dwarf ’s diet is very similar to that of well-to-do manlings. Dwarfs generally like their meat. Many Dwarf holds maintain a herd of  small, shaggy, tough mountain cattle bred from the great wild aurochs of the forested lowlands, whilst others domesticated mountain goats and sheep millennia ago. This livestock provided Dwarfs with meat, milk, pelts, and wool. In temperate climes this livestock is taken to high pastures from the month of Pflugzeit to the last week of Erntezeit, enabling the creatures to fatten up on nutritious mountain grasses. When the weather starts shifting to colder weather, the livestock return to partially underground shelters where a breeding stock is kept safe over winter. The rest of the livestock is slaughtered for meat, much of which is prepared as Kuri, heavily seasoned with spiced berries and smoked or boiled. 

Dwarfs dwelling beyond Dwarf holds within Dwarf realms are often avid hunters. They supplement the meat from livestock by hunting game animals, both big and small, and birds. Snares are usually set to catch small game while hunting parties roam the mountains for deer, mountain goats, bear, and goat-antelopes. 

Milk from livestock is generally converted to various cheeses (hard cheese, known as Chuf and prized for its ability to stay palatable on long journeys, but also soft, and crumbly varieties), cream, yoghurt, and butter. Dwarfs do not generally drink milk.Most crops grown by Dwarfs are grains that go into the production of beer and bread. Fruits and vegetables are grown on ground not given over to grain production. Typically, Dwarfs like their meat with some bite to it. Lustrian hot peppers imported during the Golden Age are popular among Dwarfs for this reason. These crops are grown on sun-facing mountain terraces in the Vaults, Grey and Black Mountains and exported to Dwarf populations in the Worlds Edge Mountains and manling lands. 

Imperial Dwarfs are not as active raising livestock or tending fields as their Karak and Norse kin. There are more than enough manling peasants and commoners to bring in the harvest or herd livestock to the abattoirs. Imperial Dwarfs focus their abilities on the various crafts. 

## **Bread**
Bread is a common component to a Dwarf ’s diet. Most Dwarfs eat bread alongside their midday or evening meal and many Dwarf travellers carry hardtack, a form of savoury biscuit that keeps for a long time but requires a strong jaw to consume, whenever they journey long distances from home. 

The Goblin Wars brought great hardships to the Dwarfs, particularly in the Worlds Edge Mountains. Crop destruction by Greenskin marauders brought many Dwarf holds to the edge of starvation. During this time of war, Dwarfs found a way to stretch their grain reserves by developing a tough bread baked from a mixture of grain (including wild varieties) with pulverised rock they called ‘rock bread’. Known as ‘Dwarf bread’ by manlings, rock bread has little nutritional value. Its purpose was to stave off hunger pangs and allow Dwarf warriors to carry on the fight. Rock bread is still eaten in lean times. 

Dwarf holds in the Worlds Edge Mountains commemorate the Goblin Wars with ritual fasting where only rock bread is eaten. 

## **Beer and Brewing**
Dwarfs view brewing as more than an art and beer as more than a drink. Dwarf brewers produce both ales and lagers. Dwarf brewmasters are held in high esteem in Dwarf society, sometimes rivalling Dwarf kings for a Dwarf hold’s affections. 

Dwarf beers are one of the most important parts of their dietary regimen. Dwarf beers are so nutritious that aDwarf can solely subsist on it for weeks at a time. Dwarf beer is called gorog in Khazalid, and is particularly potent, though this troubles these hearty folk not at all. By and large, Dwarfs are inherently better than Manlings at holding their drink, and show far fewer adverse effects, even when consuming copious amounts. Dwarf hazkal is lighter than gorog, but only marginally less alcoholic, whilst grizdal is a term for potent ale that has been fermented for at least a century, and is considered the pinnacle of the brewer’s craft. More than any other Dwarf, the abilities and foresight of brewmasters are essential to the health of any Dwarf settlement. Master brewers who fail to provide ample supply have been known to shave their heads, proclaim their dishonour, and walk the path of a Slayer. 

Most Dwarf beer found in manling lands has been brewed by Imperial Dwarfs, though true brews brought from the holds can be found — for a price. Imperial Dwarf brewmasters produce a weaker version of their beer termed grog for sale to manlings, typically saving the good stuff for fellow Dwarfs. If pressed, Dwarf brewmasters claim that properly brewed Dwarf beer is much too strong for manlings (and, really, any nonDwarf) to stomach. Even these lesser brews are usually superior to what the manlings can produce and fetch higher prices. 

## **Dwarf Law and Punishment**
The ancient tradition of law and punishment in Dwarf society is very strong. Dwarf law has remained unchanged since the tenets were handed down by the Ancestor Gods. Dwarf law is simple and direct. It contrasts sharply with the volumes of codified, and often contradictory, manling laws. Violations of Dwarf law results in swift and certain punishment with little room for appeal. 

Given their clannish ways, capital crimes among Dwarfs are extremely rare. Any Karak or Norse Dwarf accused of such a crime must appear before a tribunal of three to five judges selected by the Dwarf hold’s king (or Chief Elder of a Dwarf settlement). Imperial Dwarfs are subject to the manling laws of the jurisdiction in which the crime was committed, though longstanding agreements sometimes allow crimes within the Dwarf community to be handled by the Council of Elders. 

If no leniency is granted when the accused is declared guilty, then the convicted is executed by being beheaded or hung. If leniency is granted, then the guilty Dwarf is banished after being declared legally non-existent, expelled from the clan, with no protection under the law. Banished Dwarfs may become Slayers, assuming they live long enough from the vengeance of the victim’s kinfolk. 

A tribunal of clan elders try lesser crimes such as theft and perjury. The trial follows the same process as that for capital crimes. Punishments can vary based on the severity of the crime. Banishment may be imposed in the more extreme cases. Some sort of restitution is imposed in the vast majority of the cases. In a few cases, the punishment imposed by the judges is far less than what shamed Dwarfs impose upon themselves. The resulting dishonour from their crime may compel the guilty Dwarf to renounce their standing in the clan, give up all their possession, and become Slayers. 

Clan Elders (or group of elders, if more than one clan involved) judge crimes against property. The guilty are fined, obligated to perform a service, or sentenced to a combination of both. At times, the situation cannot be properly resolved and feuds may erupt. Feuds are often settled over many rounds of beer. Infrequently, blood is spilt, resulting in a destructive blood-feud. Bloodfeuds typically end only when a Dwarf of sufficiently high standing (such as a ranking Priest of Grungni) intervenes to bring it to an end. Guilty parties must pay compensation to any injured party or their heirs. 

Under oath to Grungni and Valaya, accused Dwarfs present their case with witnesses for and against the Dwarf providing additional testimony under the same oath. Deliberations among the judges are usually quick. Once reached, the judges give the accused one more chance to state their case. If the Dwarf confesses to the crime before a guilty pronouncement is made, then they will be granted a degree of leniency in their punishment.
